subject: Archaeology
title: The Royal Tombs of Ur
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Royal Tombs of Ur.

hook.text: Leonard Woolley opened a tomb at Ur in 1928 and found 74 servants lying in neat rows — they had been buried alive with the queen.

buildup.text: Queen Puabi's tomb held gold headdresses, lapis lazuli jewelry, a golden dagger.

discovery.text: The servants appeared to have drunk poison willingly and lay down in rows wearing their finest clothes.

twist.text: CT scans in 2009 revealed blunt force trauma on some skulls. The 'willing sacrifice' story may have been wrong all along.

climax.text: The Royal Tombs of Ur showed Sumerian wealth, artistry, and a dark ritual of royal death.

punchline.text: They wore gold and drank poison. CT scans say not everyone went willingly.

quiz.question: What did CT scans reveal about the servants in Queen Puabi's tomb?
options: They had been dead for years before being placed in the tomb
Some skulls showed blunt force trauma — not all may have gone willingly
They were wooden mannequins dressed in real clothing

details.summary: Leonard Woolley excavated the Royal Tombs of Ur in the 1920s, uncovering spectacular gold artifacts and evidence of mass human sacrifice. Dozens of attendants were buried alongside royalty, revealing extreme social hierarchy in early Sumerian civilization around 2600 BCE.
details.whyItMatters: The Royal Tombs of Ur revealed the wealth and power of early Sumerian rulers. The mass burials shocked the world and raised questions about power, belief, and the human cost of early civilization.
takeaways: Woolley excavated the Royal Tombs of Ur in the 1920s
Gold artifacts included the famous golden helmet and lyres
Mass burials showed dozens of attendants sacrificed with rulers

faq.question: What were the most important finds from the Royal Tombs?
faq.answer: The golden helmet of Meskalamdug, the Standard of Ur mosaic, golden lyres, and elaborate jewelry. The sheer quantity of gold and lapis lazuli demonstrated that Ur was a wealthy, powerful city with far-reaching trade networks by 2600 BCE.

faq.question: Why were attendants buried with the royal dead?
faq.answer: The attendants likely believed they would serve their rulers in the afterlife. They appear to have drunk poison willingly and were arranged in orderly rows. This practice reveals deep religious conviction and extreme social hierarchy in early Sumer.
